newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen dismisses U.S as king meets Asian envoys.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen dismisses U.S as king meets Asian envoys.

text.p: Cambodia's defiant Second Prime Minister Hun Sen stood his ground against criticism by Washington on Thursday as Asian foreign ministers met the country's ailing king in a bid to solve the crisis in his homeland.
Hun Sen dismissed the U.S. decision not to recognise his new co-premier, Foreign Minister Ung Huot, saying it was up to Cambodians to accept the appointment, not Americans.
"This is not so unusual," Hun Sen said. "The most important thing for us is whether Ung Huot is acceptable to our people or not. We please our people, we can't please the Americans."

Ung Huot, a senior member of ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, was on Wednesday chosen by the remnants of the royalist party to succeed Ranariddh, who was ousted in a bloody July 6 takeover.
But Washington said there was no evidence that the party had elected Ung Huot on a free and democratic basis.

Hun Sen said he backed Ung Huot's nomination. He also said he was taking measures to end human rights abuses. Diplomatic sources said some 40 opposition supporters have been tortured or killed since the prince was ousted.

In Beijing, Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines met King Norodom Sihanouk to discuss how the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) could help Cambodia, Alatas said.
The king, Ranariddh's father, is in Beijing for medical treatment.
"We (sought) the advice of King Sihanouk, not just as the constitutional king but as the father of the nation, as to how ASEAN could possibly contribute to a solution," Alatas said.
"We came away from the meeting ... encouraged by his understanding and full support for our position," he said.
ASEAN decided on July 10 to postpone Cambodia's induction to the group, originally scheduled for later this month along with Burma and Laos.
The ASEAN ministers stressed that Phnom Penh's eventual entry to the forum was not in doubt and that it remained an observer and would attend forthcoming meetings, Alatas said.

Alatas declined to give details of how ASEAN hoped to help or of the views voiced by Sihanouk, who reigns but does not rule in Cambodia and who has asked that the content of his meetings with international envoys be kept secret.

Alatas and the other foreign ministers are scheduled to meet Ranariddh in Bangkok on Friday and with Hun Sen in Cambodia on Saturday. Ranariddh left Cambodia on the eve of the fighting which led to his overthrow and has not returned.
Hun Sen said on Thursday that Sihanouk should return from Beijing.
"It is in the interests of the Cambodian people and the international community that the king has better health and returns to Cambodia," he said. "The role of the king is very important."
China on Thursday called for a peaceful solution to the political crisis in Cambodia and pledged Beijing's support for the authority and dignity of the king.

Treading cautiously among old allies and former foes in Cambodia's warring forces, Beijing promised not to become involved in the internal affairs of a nation it once saw as a Maoist ideological ally.

"All parties in Cambodia should cherish the current peaceful situation and resolve current problems to prevent a deterioration of the situation," Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang told a news briefing.
"China will never become involved in Cambodia's affairs," Tang said.
Tang would not comment on whether Beijing planned to recognise Ung Huot as Ranarridh's legitimate successor.
Vietnam on Thursday became the first country to indicate tacit approval of Ung Huot since his nomination, though Hanoi stopped short of recognising him in the new position.
The United States said on Wednesday it was "very concerned" by Ung Huot's nomination as Cambodia's new co-prime minister and did not recognise him in that role.

"We urge the authorities in Phnom Penh to refrain from announcing a new first prime minister until Prince Ranariddh's political party has an opportunity to make a reasoned decision on this matter, free of coercion, free of intimidation," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing in Washington.
Ung Huot should not accept the job without Ranariddh expressing an opinion, he added.

The United States suspended aid to Cambodia for 30 days after Ranariddh's ouster and the U.S. Senate voted 99-0 late on Wednesday to halt U.S. aid until the secretary of state certified that the Cambodian government was established by free and fair elections, and not by force or coup.
Burns also said the United States was "very deeply troubled" by the reports of killings in the aftermath of Hun Sen's ouster of his co-premier.

Ranariddh defeated former battlefield foe Hun Sen in a costly 1993 election organised by the United Nations but agreed to a power-sharing coalition with Hun Sen after a brief period of political turmoil.
